reader_notes: Reads like a long-form magazine feature (LRB / New Yorker register). Plausible as an authentic ELF long text, though at the demanding end of the range.

The physics is not just plausible, it is right: nucleating a fresh crystal needing roughly half again the vapour of maintaining one is real, and it does the argumentative work of explaining why the layers are invisible. That makes Q2 answerable from two independent places in the text.
Q3 hinges on a genuine two-effects-cancel point; C ('cools the ground instead') is a well-built trap for a reader who half-remembers the daylight clause.

Q4 is the best question here: A inverts the actual statistic (all 141 flew through a forecast layer; fewer than half left a mark), and getting to C requires carrying the over-forecasting finding across to the descents that were flown. Demanding but single-answer.

Q5 is settled by 'the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced' plus the note that the second finding 'needed no picture at all'. D overstates (he never calls for ending the imagery) and B misreads the noncommittal 'Perhaps it would'.

The final paragraph is the densest stretch in the unit. The sentence 'only one of the readings it allows blames the forecast; two are the camera's, and the fourth is the success' asks the reader to count back to the four causes of an empty frame listed a few lines earlier; I had to re-read it once. It resolves correctly and is stylistically deliberate, but it is where friction lives.

Numbers are internally consistent throughout (61 of 141; 96 of 406 flown, supporting 'most of the descents it asks for are never flown'; two percent per adjusted flight becoming a fraction of a percent across the sector).
